title: A Healthy 'Twin' Can Help Bleached Coral Recover
summary:
Scientists have found that badly bleached corals can fully recover after touching healthy corals that are genetically identical to them. In lab tests, the bleached corals got healthy again within seven weeks. The study was published on October 14 in the journal Science Advances.

Corals may look like plants or rocks, but they are animals. Tiny algae live inside their bodies and give them much of the energy they need. When ocean water gets too warm, corals lose these algae and turn white. This is called bleaching. Bleached corals are weak, and recovery can take months or years.

The idea for the study came from an accident in 2025. In the lab of Stanford professor Steve Palumbi, two pieces from the same coral, one healthy and one bleached, fell against each other in a tank. Where they touched, the bleached piece started getting its color back.

Lead author Danny Collins, a student at Stanford, then set up a test with 10 pairs of coral pieces. Each pair had one healthy piece and one bleached piece from the same coral. In five pairs, the pieces touched. In the other five, they were kept a few millimeters apart. Every bleached piece that touched its partner fully recovered. The ones kept apart died.

Palumbi explained that identical corals recognize each other and their tissues join together. Tiny channels lined up between the pieces, letting the helpful algae and food move into the bleached coral within three days. One week of contact, and sometimes just five days, was enough.

The researchers say this could lead to new ways to restore coral reefs.
why_it_matters: Warming oceans are bleaching coral reefs, which many sea creatures depend on. A fast way to help bleached corals recover could give reef restoration a useful new tool.

background_read: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which live together in large colonies.
Many corals get most of their energy from tiny algae living inside their tissues, and the algae also give corals their color.
When ocean water stays too warm, corals can push out these algae and turn white, which is called bleaching.
Many corals grow by copying themselves, so pieces of the same colony are genetically identical.
